PullRequest.Title: agentHost: observe dispatched actions through a chat contribution hook
PullRequest.Body:
agentHost: observe dispatched actions through a chat contribution hook

Moves session input-needed aggregation, turn-usage persistence, and session flag persistence
out of `AgentSideEffects`, which loses 252 lines, and closes the last gaps where a turn ended
without telling contributions.

## Dispatched-action hook

All three moved behaviors observed `AgentHostStateManager.onDidEmitEnvelope` rather than the
client dispatch path, so none could use the existing action hook: most of the actions they
react to are dispatched by the host, not by a client.

- Adds `onDidDispatchAction`, which observes an action from any origin once its outcome is
  known, including server-dispatched actions and rejected ones that never reduced. It is a
  separate hook and not a widening of the client hook, because `queueDrain` depends on that
  hook being client-only and would otherwise see each client action twice.
- Adds `SessionInputNeededContribution` (order 200), which mirrors per-chat blockers into the
  owning session's `inputNeeded` list. This is the bulk of the move at roughly 170 lines.
- Gives `PersistedTurnUsageContribution` the write half of turn-usage persistence. It already
  owned the restore half, so one contribution now owns both directions, as chat drafts and
  chat titles already do.
- Adds `SessionFlagsContribution` (order 700) for read state, archived state, and merged
  config values. It preserves an asymmetry that is easy to lose: read and archived changes
  skip a rejected action, config values do not.
- Makes `AgentHostToolCallTracker` injectable. Input-needed reports blocked and unblocked tool
  calls to it, and it was constructed inside `AgentSideEffects`, so a contribution could not
  reach it.

## Terminal turn outcomes

A turn that captured a start checkpoint and then failed to send never scheduled its changeset
recompute, because `captureTurnStartCheckpoint` runs before `sendMessage` but the catch never
reported the end.

- Reports a turn end when a send throws, which fixes that bug.
- Reports a turn end for a client-dispatched cancellation, which the agent-signal path already
  did. This fires exactly once: the reducer clears the active turn first, so a later
  agent-emitted cancellation takes the no-active-turn path, which reports only completions.
- Adds a `rejected` reason for requests refused before their turn started, fired from both
  `startTurn` early returns.
- Makes `MarkUnreadContribution` ignore `rejected`. It filtered negatively, so a rejection on
  an archived session would have marked it unread and resurfaced it.
- Leaves `QueueDrainContribution` untouched for `rejected`. A rejected queued turn consumes
  its message and the queue stalls, but draining would cascade an archived chat through every
  queued message. The fix is to return the message to the queue, which is recorded as such.

## Naming

Renames the two action hooks so each says what it observes:

- `onAction` becomes `onDidApplyClientAction`, and `IObservedAction` becomes
  `IAppliedClientAction`. Rejected client actions never reach it, so an action it sees always
  reduced.
- `onEnvelope` becomes `onDidDispatchAction`, and `IObservedEnvelope` becomes
  `IDispatchedAction`. It also delivers rejected actions, so a name claiming they were applied
  would be wrong.

## Tests and docs

Registers the built-in contributions in the tool-call and turn-hang telemetry test graphs.
Both build `AgentSideEffects` without them, so they stopped exercising blocked-call telemetry
once that reporting moved into a contribution. The graphs now mirror production wiring; no
assertion changed. Both new `agentSideEffects` tests were confirmed to fail without the
turn-end fix.

Updates the contributions skill, which described four hooks and named two that no longer
exist. It now documents all seven, records that the admission hook fails closed and is
synchronous while every other hook isolates failures, and carries the design rationale that
`TODO.md` used to hold. `TODO.md` keeps only open work and caveats, with each fact in one
place.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The synchronous call path is explicit: `_dispatchActionForSession` dispatches every streamed action, `AgentHostStateManager` fires `onDidEmitEnvelope` before returning, and the new listener calls `didDispatchAction`, whose added loop invokes the allocation-and-sort helper. Built-in registration and documentation establish roughly 17 contributions while only three implement this hook; exact stream chunk counts vary by provider but the per-envelope mechanism is certain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Array allocations and comparison/sort CPU over the complete contribution registry.
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Cost is O(A × C log C), where A is the number of emitted action envelopes (including token/reasoning/tool deltas) and C is the registered contribution count; concurrent chats multiply A. The current built-in graph has roughly 17 contributions but only three observers for this hook.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased synchronous CPU work and GC pressure on response streaming, with cost multiplied by action frequency and concurrent active chats.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The envelope listener directly ran tightly filtered input-needed, usage, and session-flag logic; it did not allocate and sort the contribution registry for every streamed action. Contribution sorting was limited to less frequent lifecycle/client-dispatch hooks.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every server or client action envelope now synchronously allocates and sorts the complete contribution registry before filtering down to the three contributions that implement `onDidDispatchAction`.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added `didDispatchAction` loop at RIGHT line 164 calls the existing `_getOrderedContributions()` helper for every envelope; that helper spreads the entire registration map into a new array and sorts it. The new call site in `AgentSideEffects` invokes this hook unconditionally from `onDidEmitEnvelope`, including `ChatDelta`, `ChatReasoning`, and tool-delta actions.
Findings.Title: Cache dispatch observers instead of sorting them per streamed action
Findings.Impact: Long or highly incremental agent responses do needless synchronous CPU work and short-lived allocation for every streamed chunk, increasing agent-host CPU/GC pressure and potentially reducing streaming throughput or responsiveness when several chats stream concurrently.
Findings.Evidence: `AgentHostChatContributions.didDispatchAction` iterates `_getOrderedContributions()` at line 164. `_getOrderedContributions()` creates `[...this._registeredContributions.values()]` and sorts it on every call. `AgentSideEffects` now calls `didDispatchAction` for every emitted envelope, and streamed `ChatDelta` actions are dispatched once per provider chunk. Therefore ordinary response streaming repeats an O(C log C) sort plus array allocation per chunk even though most contributions are immediately skipped.
Findings.Recommendation: Cache the ordered registrations and invalidate that cache only when contributions are registered or removed; preferably cache a hook-specific ordered observer list so `didDispatchAction` iterates only its three implementers. This preserves ordering and failure isolation without per-envelope sorting/allocation.

Scenarios.Scenario: Streaming an agent response with text, reasoning, and tool-call delta actions
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Provider event mapping synchronously dispatches each action through `AgentHostStateManager`; `onDidEmitEnvelope` fires before dispatch returns, and the new `didDispatchAction` hook now allocates/sorts the full contribution registry on that critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One SQLite write per non-subagent `ChatUsage` report, not per text/reasoning delta; writes for a database are sequenced.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same envelope listener already persisted each qualifying usage report with the same database open/write/dispose flow.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Database completion is fire-and-forget, although opening the cached database reference and serializing usage occur synchronously in the envelope listener.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of emitted provider action chunks across concurrently active chats; each action now also scales with the roughly 17 registered contributions because the registry is recopied and resorted.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each chat dispatches actions synchronously; multiple active chats can independently produce action streams, multiplying aggregate work. The contribution callbacks are serial and have no limiter because they execute inline.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: State reads are in-memory. Session database handles use the existing data-service reference lifecycle; no new result cache or coalescing was added. Contribution ordering is not cached, which is the reported regression.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the call path and `_getOrderedContributions()` implementation directly prove one fresh array and sort for every envelope.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Provider chunk sizes and concurrent-chat prevalence vary, so exact CPU and GC cost is unmeasured; the per-envelope allocation/sort and synchronous reachability are certain.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable medium CPU/GC regression: universal action observation moved full-registry sorting onto the streamed-action path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Tool confirmation, client execution, authentication, and chat-input blocker synchronization
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After a relevant chat action reduces, the contribution synchronously scans the active/completed turn and session `inputNeeded` list, then may dispatch one nested session action before the original envelope listener returns.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Response-part count in the addressed turn and outstanding session input requests. Effective work is one synchronization for each relevant tool/input lifecycle action.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Actions are handled synchronously and serially per JavaScript event turn. There is no external concurrency limiter because this path performs in-memory scans and state dispatch only.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Authoritative chat and session state are read from the in-memory state manager. Equality suppresses unchanged `SessionInputNeededSet` actions; removals check current state before dispatch.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the moved implementation and action filters are visible and preserve the previous algorithms and cardinality.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Very large response-part or blocker lists are possible but not established as common.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate regression: the scans and nested dispatches were moved from the same envelope listener without increasing their relevant-action frequency.

Scenarios.Scenario: Persisting session read/archive/config flags and turn usage
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Qualifying envelopes synchronously open a database reference and enqueue an asynchronous SQLite metadata or usage write; write completion is off the action-dispatch critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one metadata write for each matching flag/config action.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same `onDidEmitEnvelope` listener performed the same persistence for the same matching actions.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The write promise is fire-and-forget; reference opening and JSON serialization for config values occur synchronously.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One write per qualifying parent-chat usage report, with subagents and empty turn IDs filtered out.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical filtering and write behavior existed in `AgentSideEffects._trackTurnUsage`.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Asynchronous sequenced write; serialization and database-reference acquisition happen inline.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of matching state-change and usage-report actions, after subagent and rejection filters.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Turn-usage writes are serialized by the existing database sequencer. Metadata writes use the existing database service/connection scheduling; the PR adds no burst loop or per-collection fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Database references reuse the existing session data service; no positive/negative cache semantics changed. Usage writes remain last-report-wins and sequenced.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: before/after code is a direct extraction with unchanged operations and filters.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Usage report frequency depends on provider behavior, but the diff does not change qualifying cardinality.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: expensive database boundaries retain their previous count, placement, and asynchronous scheduling.

Scenarios.Scenario: Turn rejection, client cancellation, and provider send failure terminal handling
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Rejections synchronously notify contributions but built-ins filter them. A real client cancellation now runs bounded turn-end contributions. A send failure now asynchronously captures an end checkpoint and schedules changeset recomputation after the failed send is already known.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Capture git working-tree checkpoint for each configured repository after a non-resumable send error
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Once per actually ended failed turn, with repository operations per configured working directory.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: A thrown send did not report `onTurnEnd`, so it skipped the end checkpoint and final changeset recomputation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Fire-and-forget after failure dispatch; it does not delay reporting the failed send, though it can consume background git/DB capacity.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read/write checkpoint and changeset state during failure finalization
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Bounded to one finalization per tracked failed turn; duplicate/stale outcomes are suppressed by `turnCompleted` returning false.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No final checkpoint/changeset work ran when `sendMessage` threw.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Asynchronous and off the failed-send response path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist unread flag after a real client cancellation
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one metadata write per cancellation that actually ends a tracked turn; stale/duplicate cancellation is suppressed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Client-dispatched cancellation did not notify turn-end contributions and therefore did not trigger this unread persistence path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: State dispatch is synchronous; metadata write is fire-and-forget.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of actual failed/cancelled turns and configured working directories, not queued messages or stale terminal actions.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Turn-end contributions execute serially. Git checkpoint capture is sequenced per session; changeset computations use keyed sequencers, allowing different turn/static keys to proceed independently while serializing each key.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Tracked-turn state suppresses duplicate terminal work. Git checkpoint state and changeset sequencers retain their existing per-session/per-key coalescing and ordering behavior.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the added boundaries and duplicate suppression; low concern about product impact because work is bounded, failure-only, and off the response critical path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Send failures are exceptional and repository count varies; background git duration is workload-dependent.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: the newly reached finalization work is intentionally bounded to one real failed turn, sequenced, and asynchronous; cancellation adds only one bounded metadata write.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent-host construction and disposal after making the tool-call tracker injectable
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Core service registration installs a lazy descriptor; constructing `AgentSideEffects` and built-in contributions resolves the shared tracker at the same lifecycle stage where `AgentSideEffects` previously constructed it directly.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Tracked turns and tool calls, with existing clear/completion paths removing entries.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One shared tracker service receives synchronous lifecycle updates; no new process, worker, or remote call is created.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The tracker's maps retain the same per-turn/per-tool state and cleanup calls. Service lifetime changes ownership to the core service collection but does not create duplicate trackers in production wiring.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No meaningful magnitude uncertainty; construction timing and state structures are explicit.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance regression: object construction is relocated rather than duplicated, and cleanup paths remain present.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 25 changed files. One medium-confidence-impact/high-mechanism-confidence issue was submitted: the new universal dispatch hook recopies and sorts the complete contribution registry for every streamed action. Database persistence extractions preserve existing boundary cardinality; new terminal failure work is bounded, sequenced, and off the critical path.
